BILL NUMBER:  S6991

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the election law, in relation to a voter claiming to
live within an election district in which the voter seeks to vote
being advised of the proper polling place and election district and
being allowed to vote in said election district


 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :
To enable voters to vote in the correct polling place by providing
such items as maps, street finders or other descriptions of polling
places ensuring that their vote counts. To require a poll clerk or
election inspector to consult a map, street finder or other
description of all of the polling places in the election districts
within the county in which the election district is located in order
to advise the voter of his or her correct polling place.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :
Section one amends the section heading and subdivision 1 of section
4-128 of the election law, as amended by chapter 91 of the laws of
1992, by changing the title of the bill to now apply to the "loan
clerk" as opposed to "city or village clerk" and also requiring the
board of elections of each county to provide a sufficient number: of
maps, street finders or other descriptions of all the polling places
and election districts within the county in which the polling place is
located. Such items will enable the election inspector:s and poll
cler:ks to determine the correct election district and polling place
for each street address within the county in which the polling place
is located.

Section two amends the opening paragraph of section 4-132 of the
election law, as amended by chapter 164 of the laws of 1985, and adds
new subdivision d which adds a sufficient number of maps, street
finders or other descriptions of all polling places and election
districts within the county in which the polling place is located to
the list of things to be supplied by the board of elections or the
town or: city clerk.

Section three amends the opening paragraph of paragraph (e) of
subdivision 3 of section 8-302 of the election law, as amended by
chapter 200 of the laws of 1996, to require a poll clerk or election
inspector to consult a map, street finder or other description of all
of the polling places and election districts within the county in
which such election district is located in order to advise the voter
of his or her correct polling place and election district.

Section four defines the effective date as immediately.

 JUSTIFICATION :
The purpose of these amendments is to ensure that voters who vote by
affidavit ballot have a realistic chance to exercise the franchise. A
voter has the option of voting by affidavit ballot when the inspectors
of election (hereinafter "poll workers") cannot find the voter's
registration in the records at the polling place on election day. As
recently affirmed by the Court of Appeals in Matter of Panio v.
Sunderland, 4 NY3d 123, 791 NYS2d 57 (2005), affidavit ballots cast
b)(voters in the wrong polling place cannot be counted.  In Matter of
Panio, the Court of Appeals rejected the claim that the failure to
provide street finders for poll workers to consult before giving
voters affidavit ballots was a ministerial error by the Board of
Elections. The proposed amendments are necessary to insure that the
affidavit ballot does not become what one commentator has termed a
"placebo ballot," instead of a fail-safe method by which duly
registered voters may vote on election day, as mandated by the Help

America Vote Act (HAVA). (Ari Weisbard, "Placebo Ballots Will
'Fail-Safe' Voting Fail?," www.usa.org/pub295.cfm).

The proposed amendments to Election Law §§ 4-128 and 4-132 will insure
that poll workers are supplied with county-wide street finders to
enable them to determine whether voters are in the correct polling
place on election day. In addition, the amendment to Election Law
§B-302 will mandate that poll workers have a duty to check the street
finder prior to providing a voter with an affidavit ballot.  Affidavit
ballots are utilized by voters whose names do not appear in the
registration records. A voter's name may not appear in the
registration records because the registration poll record maybe lost
or misplaced, the voter may have been placed on "inactive" status
pursuant to Election Law §5-213, or the voter may have moved within
the county and remain eligible to vote by affidavit ballot at the
polling place for the voter's new residence (while his name remains in
the poll book for his prior address).

The Election Law does not make it easy for voters to determine where
to vote. Voters are sent a "check" card, pursuant to Election Law
§4-117(1). This card is used to verify that voters are still residing
at the address at which they registered to vote, as well as to advise
voters of a change in the location of their polling place. However,
the card must be sent more than two months before election day and it
is not sent to voters whose status is "inactive." ID. In addition,
because the check card is not forwardable, it is not received by any
voter who has moved.  ID. So, the two largest classes of voters for
whom affidavit ballots were created -- inactive voters and voters who
have moved will never receive the cards advising them where to vote,
and those voters who do receive them, will get them at some time prior
to Labor Day for an election to take place in November.

For a voter who has never received notification of where to vote, or
did so months before election day, it is not a simple process to go to
the right polling place. And in the absence of a comprehensive street
finder, a poll worker lacks the tools to direct a voter- who has ended
up in the wrong place on election day.  The poll workers provide the
affidavit ballot to the voter. Prior to providing it to a voter whose
name does not appear in the registration records for that polling
place, Election Law §8-302 (1) currently provides that the poll
workers have the responsibility of "verifying the right of persons to
vote." However, the Election Law does not require that the poll
workers ascertain whether the voter is in the polling place assigned
for his or her address prior to giving the voter an affidavit ballot.
And although the Board of Elections is required to provide poll
workers with "a map or certified description of the election district
and adjoining election districts" Election Law §5-502(1), that is
insufficient to direct a voter to the correct polling place if the
voter resides elsewhere in the county.  In Matter of Panio, supra. 457
affidavit ballots cast by duly registered voters who were in the wrong
polling place were rejected in a race that was decided by 18 votes.
The evidence presented at the trial showed that in one municipality
the poll workers received at most only a few pages of street finders,
rather than a comprehensive list, and that some poll workers received
no street finders at all (Trial Transcript, pp. 1322, 231-232). As a
result, if the poll workers could not find a voter's name in their
poll book, they could not determine whether the voter was in the right
polling place. These voters were effectively disenfranchised.

An affidavit ballot is not a realistic alternative if it has no chance
of being counted because the voter casts it in the wrong polling
place.  It is incumbent upon the Legislature to insure that poll
workers have street finders to enable them to direct voters to the
correct place and to mandate that poll workers consult the street
finder before supplying a voter with an affidavit ballot.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
2008: S.6991 - Died Elections Committee

 FISCAL IMPLICATION :
None to the state.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.
